items.body: This new recording opens with a rarity, Johan Wagenaar’s Cyrano de Bergerac Overture. Wagenaar was an important teacher and composer in Utrecht, but by the 1920s his late-Romantic style was considered outdated, and his music received scant attention outside the Netherlands. The overture’s soaring melodies, opulent harmonies, and bold orchestration show the influence of both Berlioz and Strauss, though I would argue that Wagenaar has his own distinct voice. Symphony No. 9 Amazon Presto Apple Shani leads an exciting reading, with carefully balanced textures that let us appreciate the music’s contrapuntal complexity. He shapes the music well and encourages some resplendent brass at climaxes. Two other excellent performances both feature the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra: Mengelberg in 1942, available on YouTube, and Chailly (1990/Decca). Neither is easy to find on CD today (though both can be streamed at Presto or Amazon), so Shani’s performance has the field to itself. Presto lists over 400 recordings of Dvořák’s final symphony; in an overly crowded field, a new recording should offer something that challenges or exceeds what is already available. In recent years I reviewed performances by the Czech Philharmonic (Bychkov/Pentatone – review) and the Atlanta Symphony Orchestra (Stutzmann/Erato – review). Bychkov’s reading is beautifully played and recorded, but emotional engagement comes and goes. The Atlanta orchestra does not match the sophisticated sheen of their Czech counterparts, but Stutzmann’s emotional connection is complete, and she takes interpretive risks that, even after repeated hearings, never strike me as mannered or willful. I find her reading exciting, spontaneous, and compelling. This performance shows the Rotterdam orchestra in top form. The conducting and engineering ensure a transparency that reveals the inner workings of Dvořák’s score. Shani honors the score’s markings and leads with an excellent sense of structure. Nothing in this interpretation feels mannered or willful. Yet, despite these positive qualities, Shani’s reading does not really stand out from other similarly well-executed recordings. Lack of forward drive is a significant issue. For instance, in the opening movement’s transition from Adagio to Allegro molto (circa 0’55”), brass and timpani speak resoundingly. But the articulation needs the cut and thrust heard in readings by Rafael Kubelík (Berlin PO/DG), Andris Nelsons (Bavarian RSO/BR Klassik), and Charles Mackerras (Prague SO/Supraphon). Each of these imparts a greater sense of anticipation and urgency. The same issue afflicts the remainder of the movement. The molto indication is not really honored: the performance focuses instead on balance and beauty of sound at the expense of momentum. Kubelík, Nelsons, and Mackerras are also balanced and beautiful, but they have a drive and excitement that is lacking in Shani’s reading. The second movement (13’13”) is quite slow. By comparison, Bychkov takes 11’12” (a particularly beautiful rendition, especially the English horn); Mackerras, 12’21”; and Giulini (Philharmonia/Warner Classics), 12’33”. All of these readings are sweetly sung, but there is greater passion in the older readings. Kubelík is almost as slow as Shani, but the Rotterdam orchestra cannot match the finesse and richness of the Berliners. Lahav Shani. Photo © Marco Borggreve. I find the Scherzo far more successful: here is the energy and joie de vivre I missed in the opening movement. The Trio has a delightful lilt and range of colors. Yet turn to both Nelsons and Stutzmann, and one can hear more turbulent passions than are heard here. Similar issues affect the final movement. The problem is not one of tempo: Shani’s timing of 11’40” is only two seconds shorter than Dudamel’s recent Los Angeles performance (DG, a digital-only recording of the final three symphonies that has not had the recognition it deserves). The playing is undeniably excellent, and there is greater furor. But turn to Dudamel, or the other recordings mentioned above, to hear readings with an inexorable flow missing from the present performance. The lack of momentum affects the emotional power of this reading: with Shani, the passage around 1’55” feels gentle and pretty. Under Nelsons and Dudamel, the tempo change (and shift in mood) is more potent. Wind solos, both here and throughout the symphony, are beautifully played, but they lack the individual flair of their colleagues in Berlin, Los Angeles, and Prague. I admire the freshness and lack of mannerisms: Shani never strives to make interpretive points that go against the score. But I want more vigor and more unbridled excitement in a performance of this symphony. Despite the excellence of the playing, if I had to choose between this ‘moderate’ interpretation and the similarly conceived Bychkov/Czech Philharmonic recording, I would choose the latter. Readers who prefer a more relaxed approach may find more to admire and enjoy than I did. 2026 Weverse Con Festival brings together a record-breaking 34,000 fans through the power of music, marking its biggest edition yet.

Now in its fourth year, Weverse Con reached new milestones with its largest audience and artist lineup to date, bringing together 30 artists across multiple stages. Hosted by HYBE, the festival concluded over the weekend after drawing a record-breaking number of online and in-person attendees.

Weverse Con transformed into a “Newtopia,” immersing attendees in a vibrant musical soundscape where artists and fans came together through their shared love of music. Across KSPO DOME and the 88 Lawn Field, audiences were treated to performances that spanned genres, generations, and borders.

The festival’s lineup featured headliners LUCY, ENHYPEN, KWON JIN AH, ZICO, BOYNEXTDOOR, and HIGHLIGHT, who delivered standout performances throughout the weekend.

ENHYPEN

BOYNEXTDOOR

HIGHLIGHT

Across the two days, they were joined by a diverse mix of talented regional artists like day one's fiery lineup that featured QWER, ILLIT, Apink,  PLAVE, 82 MAJOR, AMPERS&ONE, WENDY, AHOF, HA HYUN SANG and HWANG MIN HYUN.

ILLIT

PLAVE

AHOF

Day two brought the energy tenfold with a star-studded roster featuring &TEAM, CORTIS, KIM JAE JOONG, LE SSERAFIM, P1Harmony, TWS, aoen, CUTIE STREET, KWON JIN AH, TOUCHED, YOON SAN-HA, AND2BLE, LEECHANGSUB and ZICO. The diverse mix of K-pop, J-pop, bands, singer-songwriters, and virtual artists reflects Weverse Con’s growing ambition as a festival that brings different corners of music culture together.

LE SSERAFIM

CORTIS

AND2BLE

One of the greatest highlights of this year’s festival was the Tribute Stage honouring RAIN. Reimagined by a diverse lineup of artists from different generations and musical backgrounds, the stage celebrated the enduring influence of one of Korea’s most iconic performers while capturing the essence of musical connection and discovery that lies at the core of Weverse Con’s spirit.

RAIN

Beyond the performances, fans also explored a variety of festival experiences inspired by “Newtopia,” including the Weverse Booth, Torriden Booth, Upbit Booth, and other interactive activities throughout the venue. Together, these activations helped transform Weverse Con into more than just a concert, offering fans new ways to connect with artists, fellow attendees, and the wider festival community.

“This year’s Weverse Con Festival offered music fans from Korea and around the world a diverse musical experience through its expanded stage programming, enhanced production, and largest-ever lineup spanning genres and generations,” HYBE shared in a statement. “We will continue to grow Weverse Con as a global music festival that showcases the value and appeal of Korean popular music while delivering distinctive live experiences for audiences worldwide.”

With its record-breaking attendance, expanded lineup, and cross-generational celebration of music, 2026 Weverse Con Festival marks another milestone in the festival’s growing journey as a global live music event.

items.body: Jowee Omicil sMiLes (Bash Village - digital release) Review by Michael Stone sMiLes by Jowee Omicil B orn in Montreal, Haitian-Canadian musician-composer Jowee Omicil plays a fabulous variety of saxophones, clarinets, trumpets, flutes, piano, and keyboards. He came of age in the choral milieu of his father’s Montreal congregation, studied saxophone and music education at Berklee, and gleaned much from engagement with figures including Wyclef Jean, Tony Allen, Ibrahim Maalouf, Roy Hargrove, Kenny Garrett, Pharoah Sanders, Branford Marsalis, and Marcus Miller among others. Over the course of 2025, Omicil released sMiLes one song per month, each accompanied by a philosophizing podcast. The album opens with a striking reinterpretation of singer and Civil Rights activist Abbey Lincoln’s “Throw It Away,” whose message Omicil invokes in his voiceover, an expression of kinship in creative philosophical outlook. (For good measure, Omicil revisits the title on a distinctive “Throw it Away - FuLL oF LoVe Remix.”) Lincoln’s own 2007 rendition on Abbey Sings (Verve) offers critical context, itself worth a comparative audition for the original melody and the contemplative character of her lyrics. Throw it away, throw it away Give your love, live your life, each and every day And keep your hand wide open, let the sun shine through, Because you can never lose a thing, if it belongs to you. In less accomplished hands, the quirky sampling, effects, instrumentation, and wide-ranging, scruffy, sonic bricolage of sMiLes could make for one muddy mélange. But no danger lies here in Jowee’s paradoxical, provocative, sound-shifting extended groove. Omicil's voice and sax blend almost imperceptibly in “SOeuR FeLiX AKA BeeHive.” In “Trip to GHanA,” polyrhythm meets wah-tone high-life guitar, cackly sax, and wordless vocalise. sMiLes by Jowee Omicil sMiLes by Jowee Omicil Feat. Mawuena Kodjovi Other titles transport the listener to Haiti, Morocco, Cape Verde, Jupiter, and Mali. “LeTTre Du MALi PouR JonaTHan” is a meditative, revelatory piano solo nearly ten minutes in length. sMiLes by Jowee Omicil sMiLes may invoke the free-blowing spirit of Miles (as on the sound-effected “MiLes ConvoY”), but there is no anxiety of influence here. Far from a rote genuflection to musical antecedents, the prevailing voice throughout is purely Omicil’s. As he counsels, “trust the note.” "Seek for the sound that is within you and the [instrument] will drive you to your destination… the singularity of sound is what I have always been searching for, the sound that comes from the heart, the sound that maybe, perhaps, is only heard in nature, this is what we are looking for when we are talking about sound… deep down, heartfelt uniqueness, always connected with the spirits…" - Jowee Omicil In accord with his music education formation, Omicil also leads music workshops through his BasH! AkademY, “a close-knit setting embracing spontaneity, authenticity, and shared growth,” which in 2025 included “a nomadic music experience traveling the world” to Mindelo, Cabo Verde. In 2026 Omicil will perform in New York, Canada, Martinique, France, Germany, Austria, Poland, Romania, the UK, and an African tour in the planning stage. Find the artist online.
